I would treat this as an urgent payroll exception, not let the noon automation make an unchecked dismissal decision.

Under the **codes as stated**, Ryan’s absence is not SC: he says he was not ill. It is not BRV, and his sister does not fit the listed DEP relationships or household rule. So the provisional code is **UA**. I would not use another code simply to avoid the probation consequence. I would add a brief, factual note recording that he says he took his sister to hospital during labour and rang Gary at 5:40.

But I would **not allow that code to trigger the termination letter without urgent human review**. At 11:40 I would email payroll, the HR Manager and Gary, flag the noon deadline, and ask payroll to hold Ryan’s row or suppress the letter pending review. His prompt call matters to the contract’s stated purpose of ensuring starters tell their team leader when they cannot attend. HR should also check whether any wider policy or statutory right concerning time off for dependants applies; the internal DEP definition given here does not settle that question.

If a hold is available, I would keep the coding accurate while the employment decision is reviewed. If it is not, I would escalate immediately to an available authorised person and seek a Ryan-specific pause rather than disguise the absence with a false code. The facts support a provisional code, but an automated payroll consequence should not substitute for review of whether dismissal is appropriate.
